To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cytoskeletal proteins, radixin (a protein that binds to the cytoplasmic domain of the adhesion molecule, CD44), cofilin (a protein involved in actin polymerization) and centractin (a protein that is involved in the transport of cytoskeletal elements), are abnormally expressed in MPTP-treated mouse models and that these cytoskeletal proteins are under DA control in GT1-7 cells through specific D1 dopamine receptors.
MPTP-treatments in mice lead to changes in the expression of cytoskeletal protein genes in the striatum and that these changes are linked to dopaminergic signaling.
MPTP treatment induces changes in cytoskeletal genes expression in the striatum and radixin mRNA levels are under DA regulation through specific dopaminergic receptors

the identification of new genes that could contribute to the understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease and the development of new strategies for treatment.
the identification of the molecular mechanisms involved in DA-regulated gene expression and the possible involvement of cytoskeletal genes in Parkinson's disease.

the cytoskeletal proteins radixin, cokin and centractin are under DA control in the striatum and that the abnormal expression of these proteins in the MPTP-treated mouse model may be linked to the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease.
the changes in cytoskeletal protein expression in the striatum could be related to the DA deficiency in Parkinson's disease.
the cytoskeleton is a key element in the DA system, and that the DA system is a key regulator of the cytoskeletal system.

cytoskeleton proteins may have an important role in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease.
